unit.title: Scams and how to spot them
unit.description: Unauthorised firms, Ponzi schemes, pump and dump, phishing, finfluencers and what to do if you get scammed

texts: A call from London
Víctor
Your phone rings. A number starting with +44.
Hello, this is Víctor from Vandermeer Invest, in London.
We have a currency opportunity: **4 % a month, guaranteed**. Today only.
Just install AnyDesk and I'll open the account for you. Keeps things simple.
What do you do?
I install AnyDesk so he can help me
With remote access he can use your online banking as if he were you.
I hang up and look the name up on cnmv.es
Nice! Unsolicited contact, guaranteed returns, pressure and remote access: four red flags.
I ask him to email me the information
A slick PDF is easy to copy. Only the CNMV registers tell you whether a firm is authorised.
If you fall for it, you'll watch your balance grow… and you won't be able to withdraw it without paying first.
Red flag or normal?
Eight things that can happen when someone offers you an investment. Which ones are **red flags**?
Red flag
Normal for a legitimate firm
They call you without you asking
Legitimate firms don't cold-call you to sell you investments.
High, guaranteed returns
Return and risk go together: «high and safe» doesn't exist.
It's listed in the registers of authorised firms on cnmv.es
That's what a legal firm should have (though it doesn't guarantee the investment will go well).
«Today only»: they rush you
The rush is there so you don't check anything.
They ask you to install AnyDesk or TeamViewer
With remote access they can use your online banking as if they were you.
They give you the risks and costs in writing
A legal firm has to explain the risks and costs to you.
They ask you to send money abroad or pay in crypto
That makes the money much harder to trace and get back.
To withdraw your balance, you first have to pay «taxes»
«Pay to withdraw» is the ultimate red flag: that balance doesn't exist.
Sort the eight situations.
An **unauthorised firm** (a «chiringuito», as they say in Spain) offers investments **with no authorisation**. Just one of these red flags is enough to hang up and check on cnmv.es.
Ask yourself: would your usual bank do this?
Expert eye! Nobody's fooling you now.
Red flag or normal? Tap the group

steps.title: Always check
steps.body:
Unauthorised firms usually have very professional websites, English-sounding names and very friendly «advisers». Every year the CNMV (Spain's securities regulator) publishes hundreds of **warnings** about unauthorised firms.

Before investing, look the firm up on **cnmv.es**: in the registers of authorised firms and in the warnings list. Never trust what its own website says.

Nobody who knew a safe way to make 20 % a month would call you up to tell you about it.
steps.key: If someone contacts you unprompted offering high, safe returns, it's almost certainly a scam.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, check how much the S&P 500 has risen in the last year.

texts: The investment club
Sara
I've been in an investment club for two months and I've made 15 %!
Look, here are the payouts. And if you bring in two friends, you get a bonus.
What do you do?
I join: the payouts are real
In a Ponzi the first people in really do get paid… with the newcomers' money.
I ask where the returns come from and look it up with the CNMV
Good. Someone getting paid proves nothing: a Ponzi pays out as long as money keeps coming in.
I join just to bring in friends and get the bonus
Earning by recruiting is a **pyramid scheme**: you get paid with what your friends lose.
Six months later, new members stop joining.
They won't let me withdraw anything. They say it's «temporary».
With no new money, it collapses. It happened to Madoff, Fórum Filatélico and Afinsa.
10 % a month
The club promises **10 % a month**. Doesn't sound like much… Imagine it were true and you let **€1,000** grow.
At 10 % a month, compounded, how much would you have after a year?
About €2,200
About €3,140
About €1,100
1.1¹² ≈ 3.14: **about €3,140**, +214 % in a year. Compounded, it grows more than 12 × 10 %.
See what that €1,000 would turn into in 5 years.
**10 % a month** is more than **200 % a year**, and 1 % a day multiplies your money by 37 in a year. **Nothing legal delivers that consistently**: if the maths doesn't add up, it's a scam.
Over €300,000 from €1,000. Who could pay that?
Over €30,000 in three years. Does that sound realistic?
Drag the years and watch the number

steps.title: Real cases
steps.body:
• **Charles Ponzi**, Boston, 1920: he promised **50 % in 45 days**.
• **Bernard Madoff**, uncovered in 2008: for decades he fooled even professional investors.
• **Fórum Filatélico and Afinsa**, Spain, 2006: hundreds of thousands of victims of a stamp business.

A **Ponzi** pays earlier investors with newcomers' money; in a **pyramid** you earn mainly by recruiting.
steps.key: If the maths doesn't work with compound interest, it isn't a business: it's a scam.
steps.tip: Try it: open the S&P 500 with monthly candles. Real markets have red months too.

u32l3.title: Pump and dump and signal groups

texts: VIP signals
Group admin
ATTENTION: at 20:00 we reveal the coin. Everyone buy at the same time. Target x10.
20:00. The signal arrives.
The coin is ZPX. BUY NOW AND HOLD!
By 20:10 it's already up 300 %.
What do you do?
I buy now, before it goes up more
If it's already up 300 %, the organisers are selling. You'd be their buyer.
I don't buy: if I'm only hearing about it now, I'm too late
That's it! They bought earlier, quietly. Now they're selling to people like you.
I buy a little and sell quickly
Trying to be faster than the people running the game is an almost certain loss.
By 20:25 the price is back where it was.
Pump it up, then dump it: **pump and dump**. It's market manipulation, and it's banned.
Pump or serious analysis?
Messages from investing groups. Do they smell like a **pump and dump** or like serious analysis?
Smells like a pump
Serious analysis
A set time for everyone to buy at once
Everyone buying at once is the very definition of manipulation.
A tiny coin with very little volume
With low volume, a handful of purchases sends the price flying.
It explains the business, its figures and its risks
Serious analysis explains risks; manipulation only promises rockets.
Target «x10» or «x100» this week
Absurd targets to make you buy in a rush.
Premium «VIP signals» group for €99 a month
They usually make money from your fee and your purchase, not from getting calls right.
It warns that you could lose everything you invest
Warning about risk is what people who inform you properly do.
Sort the six messages.

«VIP signals» groups usually make money from **your fee and your purchase**, not from getting calls right. Pumping up a price is **market manipulation**: banned on stock exchanges and, under the EU's MiCA regulation, in crypto too.
Hint: does it explain risks or just promise rockets?
Sort each message

steps.title: Pump it, dump it
steps.body:
1. The organisers quietly buy a small asset (a crypto or a thinly traded share).
2. They announce it as «the signal» on Telegram, WhatsApp or social media.
3. Members buy and the price shoots up.
4. The organisers sell at the top.
5. The price crashes and the latecomers lose.
steps.key: If you're tipped off at the same time as thousands of people, you're not the one buying early: you're the one buying high.
steps.tip: Try it: if something shoots up, set a price alert and decide calmly tomorrow.

texts: A call from «your bank»
Bank security
Your phone rings. Your bank's number comes up on the screen.
Good afternoon. We can see an €890 purchase from an online shop. Did you make it?
No…
Don't worry, we'll cancel it. You'll get a code by text: read it out to us to cancel it.
What do you do?
I give him the code
That code **authorises** a transaction. If you give it, you're authorising the theft yourself.
I hang up and call the bank's official number myself
Perfect. Your bank will never ask for passwords or codes over the phone.
I ask him to prove he's from the bank
They may know your name and fake the number (spoofing). Hang up and call them yourself.
This is **vishing**. By text it's called smishing; by email, phishing.
Does it protect you or expose you?
Seven habits. Which ones **protect** you from phishing and which leave you **exposed**?
Protects you
Exposes you
Turning on two-step verification
With it, a stolen password isn't enough to get in.
Paying €1.99 in «fees» for a parcel you weren't expecting
A smishing classic: they're after your card details.
Logging in to your bank through its official app
You go to the official channel yourself, instead of following the path they lay out for you.
Using the same password for everything
If they steal one, every door is open.
Tapping a link to «unlock your account within 1 hour»
The rush is the bait: open the app yourself and check.
A different password for each service
If one leaks, the rest stay safe.
An email from the «tax office» asks for your card to refund you €312
Nobody needs your card to give you money back.
Sort the seven habits.

Phishing (email), smishing (text), vishing (call) and spoofing (fake sender or number) are all after the same thing: **your passwords, your codes or a transfer**. Protect yourself by going to the official channel yourself and with **two-step verification**.
Hint: are you going to the bank, or is a link taking you there?
Sort each habit

steps.title: If you've already fallen for it
steps.body:
Call your bank on its official number to block the card or the transaction, change your passwords, check your account activity and report it. You can get help on **017**, the free cybersecurity helpline run by INCIBE (Spain's national cybersecurity institute).

And when you're being rushed («your account will be blocked in 1 hour»), stop and check.
steps.key: No bank will ever ask for your passwords or codes: whoever asks for them is robbing you.
steps.tip: Try it: tell your tutor Lumi about a strange message you have received.

texts: Live off trading in 3 months
@vivirdeltrading
A year ago I was a delivery rider. Today I live off trading. A million followers know it.
My course costs €997: in 3 months you'll be living off this. And in my group I tell you what to buy.
Just so you know: this isn't financial advice.
What do you think?
With a million followers, he must know what he's doing
Followers measure popularity, not returns. His guaranteed income is the course.
He makes money selling the course, not necessarily trading
Exactly. When the product is the course, the business is you.
I'd ask him to show his losses too
Good question. And be wary of anyone promising you'll live off trading in 3 months.
Saying «this isn't advice» **doesn't protect him** if in practice he's telling you what to buy.
Are they allowed to?
An influencer can teach you a lot, but there are **red lines**. What's legitimate and what isn't?
Legitimate
Red line
Explaining what an index fund is
Teaching is free: it needs no authorisation.
Telling you what to buy based on your salary and savings
That's personalised advice: it requires CNMV authorisation.
Promoting a platform without saying they're paid
If they're paid, they have to make it clear it's advertising.
«#ad: this platform is paying me for this video»
That's the way: they flag it as advertising.
Promoting a crypto without warning about the risks
Under MiCA, crypto advertising must be clear, not misleading and warn about the risks.
Showing their portfolio and disclosing their conflicts of interest
Sharing their experience transparently is legitimate.
Getting paid for every sign-up through their link, without saying so
They win even if you lose: it's a hidden conflict of interest.
Sort the seven posts.
Teaching is free; **advising you** on what to buy based on your situation requires CNMV authorisation. And if they're paid to talk about a product, they have to say it's **advertising**.
Ask yourself: are they teaching me or telling me what to buy?
Legitimate or red line?

steps.title: Questions to ask yourself
steps.body:
Do they make money if I buy? Do they show me their losses or only their wins? Are they selling me a course or «signals»? Are they rushing me? Lots of followers doesn't mean they know how to invest.

Since 2024, crypto advertising in the EU has been regulated by **MiCA**: clear, fair, not misleading, identified as advertising and with a risk warning. At the end of 2024 the CNMV repealed its 2022 circular on crypto-asset advertising, because MiCA already regulates it across the EU.
steps.key: An influencer can teach you; if they tell you what to buy, ask yourself who's paying them.
steps.tip: Try it: if an influencer recommends a stock, add it to Favourites and follow it for a month.

texts: «Pay and you can withdraw»
TradeNova support
Recovery firm
Your balance is €14,250. To withdraw it, you must first pay €2,000 in taxes.
What do you do?
I pay: that way I get it all back
It's the last trick before they vanish. Next they'll ask for another «fee».
I don't pay anything more, I keep evidence and tell my bank
Good. No legal firm charges taxes up front before letting you withdraw.
I take out a loan to pay it
You'd be adding debt to the scam.
A week later, another message.
We recover money lost to scams. Just €1,500 in fees up front.
The **second scam**: they charge up front and disappear. They're often the same people.
Where do you go?
Every problem has its place. Where do you go **first**?
Your bank or broker
Police or Guardia Civil
CNMV or Banco de España
An hour ago you made a transfer to a scammer
Telling your bank as soon as possible can stop the transfer or block the card.
An unauthorised investment website has scammed you
Report it with all your evidence. And tell the CNMV too.
Your authorised broker rejects your complaint
After complaining to its customer service department, you can go to the CNMV.
Your bank rejects your complaint about a fee
After its customer service department, the next step is the Banco de España.
You spot strange purchases on your card
Block it now by calling your bank's official number.
A fake «lawyer» asks you for €1,500 to recover your money
It's a second scam: report it.
Place the six cases.

**First, stop the bleeding** and tell your bank; then, evidence and a police report. With an authorised firm, complain to it first and then to the **CNMV** or the **Banco de España**; for cybersecurity, INCIBE's **017**.
Do you need to stop the money now, report it or complain to a firm?
Tap where you'd go

steps.title: What to do right now
steps.body:
1. **Don't send any more money**, even if they promise to return what you've already paid.
2. **Tell your bank** as soon as possible: sometimes a transfer can be stopped.
3. **Keep evidence:** screenshots, chats, emails, payment receipts, websites.
4. **Report it** to the Policía Nacional or the Guardia Civil.
5. **Notify the CNMV** if it was an unauthorised firm.

Getting scammed doesn't make you stupid: it makes you human. Reporting it helps stop it happening to someone else.
steps.key: Stop the damage, keep evidence and report it. And be wary of anyone offering to recover your money in exchange for money.
steps.tip: Try it: tell your tutor Lumi about a case and ask her where to go first.

options: Your annual tax report is now available in the app.

u32l1-2.prompt: Put in order how to check a firm before giving it money.
options: Look it up in the official registers on cnmv.es
Check the CNMV's warnings list
If it isn't authorised, don't invest
Write down its exact name and website
u32l1-2.explanation: Always on the CNMV website, never on the firm's own.

options: A legal fund with lots of fees
A cheap broker
A firm that offers investments without authorisation
u32l1-3.explanation: It can have a flawless website and still not be authorised.

u32l1-4.prompt: Which ones are red flags? Select all that apply.
options: It sends you the contract before you sign
Very high guaranteed returns
It appears as authorised in the cnmv.es registers
They ask you to install remote access software
u32l1-4.explanation: Very high guaranteed returns and being asked to install remote access software are red flags, as is not being able to withdraw your balance without paying first. Being in the official registers and sending the contract before you sign is normal for a legal firm (although it doesn't guarantee an investment will go well).

u32l1-7.prompt: To check whether a firm is authorised, search the ____ website.
options: AEAT
OCU
DGT
CNMV

u32l1-10.prompt: A stranger has messaged Lumi on Instagram saying she makes 3 % a day, and sent her a link. What do you say?
options: Don't tap it: look the platform up on the CNMV and be wary of that profile
Give her your details so she can help you get started
Sign up, you might get lucky
u32l1-10.explanation: Unsolicited contact + impossible returns = scam, even if it comes with a smile.
feedback: Nice! «Friends» who end up recommending a platform are a very common scam.
Your details are exactly what they're after.
3 % a day doesn't exist: it's a textbook scam, often with a fake profile.
lines: A really nice girl messaged me on Instagram 😍
She says she makes 3 % a day on a platform and sent me the link.

u32l2-1.prompt: How does a Ponzi scheme pay its early investors?
options: With new investors' money
With government loans
With profits from a real business
u32l2-1.explanation: That's why it needs new money coming in non-stop.

u32l2-4.prompt: Select the messages that smell like a Ponzi or a pyramid scheme.
options: Fixed return of 2 % a week. Our traders never lose.
Your deposit at 2 % APR matures on 15 March.
Return over the last year: −4 %. Past performance is no guarantee of future returns.
Pay €300 to join and earn €100 for every friend you bring. With 10 friends you reach gold level!
u32l2-4.explanation: Earning by recruiting and sky-high fixed returns with no explanation of where they come from are their typical signs.

u32l2-5.prompt: Is it more typical of a Ponzi or a pyramid scheme?
options: You earn mainly by bringing in new members
Sky-high fixed returns with no explanation of where they come from
There are levels depending on how many people you recruit
They say they invest your money in something secret and very profitable
u32l2-5.explanation: Both need new money to pay the old investors; what changes is the hook.

u32l2-8.prompt: A Ponzi scheme pays old investors with money from ____.
options: banks
fund managers
dividends
new investors
u32l2-8.explanation: When new ones stop arriving, the house of cards collapses.

u32l2-9.prompt: What did the Bernard Madoff case, uncovered in 2008, show?
options: That a Ponzi can last decades
That Ponzi schemes only fool beginners
That the CNMV exposed it in Spain
u32l2-9.explanation: He delivered suspiciously steady returns year after year. Too regular is also a red flag.

u32l3-1.prompt: Put the stages of a pump and dump in order.
options: Members buy and the price shoots up
The price crashes
They post «the signal» in the group
The organisers quietly buy
The organisers sell at the top
u32l3-1.explanation: The organisers win because they get in before you and get out before you.

u32l3-2.prompt: Select the messages typical of a pump and dump.
options: This $0.002 crypto is going x100 this week. Last places in the premium group for €99.
Reminder: crypto-assets are very volatile and you can lose everything you invest.
The ECB leaves interest rates unchanged.
ATTENTION: at 20:00 we announce the coin. Everyone buy at the same time and HOLD. Target x10.
u32l3-2.explanation: A set time for everyone to buy at once, absurd targets and premium fees: pure manipulation.

u32l3-5.prompt: Which signs give away a pump and dump group? Select all that apply.
options: Warnings that you could lose everything
Explanations with company data and its risks
Targets like «x10» or «x100»
A set time for everyone to buy at once
u32l3-5.explanation: A set time for everyone to buy at once and targets like «x10» give manipulation away, almost always with very small assets. Serious analysis explains data and risks; manipulation only promises rockets.

u32l3-8.prompt: The strategy of inflating a price and selling at the top is called pump and ____.
options: buy
pay
hold
dump

u32l3-9.prompt: In a pump and dump, who usually wins?
options: The organisers
Those who buy on the signal
Everyone, if nobody sells
u32l3-9.explanation: Some people's profit is the loss of those who arrive later.

u32l3-11.prompt: A tiny crypto on your watchlist rises 300 % in an hour, with no news at all. On a forum, hundreds of messages shout «to the moon!». What do you do?
options: I don't buy and look for official news
I buy now, before it gets away
I buy with borrowed money to make more in less time
u32l3-11.explanation: A huge rise with no news and euphoria on social media is the typical footprint of a pump and dump. «I buy before it gets away» fails because arriving with the crowd means arriving late.
feedback: Good: if there is nothing official behind it, it is most likely an inflated rise that unwinds just as fast.
With no news to explain it and euphoria on a forum, it looks like a pump: you would be buying just as the organisers sell.
If the price goes back to where it was, the loss stays and so does the debt.

u32l4-1.prompt: Select the messages that are phishing or smishing.
options: Your monthly statement is now available in the app.
You have a refund of €312. Enter your card details to receive it.
Your parcel is being held. Pay €1.99 in fees at this link to receive it.
We've detected suspicious access. Verify your identity here within 1 hour or we'll block your account: bit.ly/…
You've made a purchase of €23.40 at a supermarket.
u32l4-1.explanation: Shortened links, urgency, «pay a fee» and «give us your card so we can refund you» are classic signs.

u32l4-2.prompt: What protects you from phishing? Select all that apply.
options: Typing the address yourself
Tapping links in text messages to save time
Using the same password so you don't forget it
Turning on two-step verification
u32l4-2.explanation: Typing the address yourself and turning on two-step verification protect you, as does using different passwords. Links in unexpected messages are the most common way in, and reusing a password turns one theft into several.

u32l4-4.prompt: Match each technique with how it reaches you.
options: Phishing
Smishing
Vishing
Spoofing
u32l4-4.explanation: The channel changes, not the goal: your passwords or your money.
right: By faking the sender or the number

u32l4-8.prompt: You tap a link in a text message and enter your broker password. You realise straight away. What do you do first?
options: Change the password and tell your broker
Delete the text and forget about it
Wait a few days and see if anything odd happens
u32l4-8.explanation: Act fast: change your passwords, tell the provider and check your transactions.
feedback: Good: you cut off access and the provider can monitor or block transactions.
Deleting the message doesn't delete what they already have.
Every minute counts: they could get in and move your money.

u32l4-9.prompt: Put in order what to do if you've given your bank details to a scammer.
options: Change your passwords
Report it to the police or the Guardia Civil
Check the transactions on your accounts
Call the bank on its official number and block everything
u32l4-9.explanation: First stop the damage, then sort things out and report it.

u32l4-10.prompt: Asking for a password plus a code that only you have is called two-____ verification.
options: key
month
bank
step
u32l4-10.explanation: With it, a stolen password isn't enough.

u32l5-1.prompt: What can an influencer do without CNMV authorisation?
options: Tell you which shares to buy based on your salary and savings
Explain what an ETF or compound interest is
Manage your money
u32l5-1.explanation: Educating is open to anyone; personalised advice requires authorisation.

u32l5-2.prompt: Select the posts that break the rules or are a trap.
options: Today I'm explaining diversification with an example. This isn't an investment recommendation.
#ad This platform is paying me for this video. Remember you can lose money.
DM me your salary and savings and I'll tell you exactly what to buy 💸
This coin is going x50! Link in bio to buy it 🚀🚀 (doesn't say they're paid to promote it)
u32l5-2.explanation: Hidden promotion and personalised advice without authorisation are the two red lines.

u32l5-6.prompt: Which questions protect you when dealing with a finfluencer? Select all that apply.
options: Do they sound very confident?
How many followers do they have?
Are they rushing me to buy?
Do they make money if I buy?
u32l5-6.explanation: Ask whether they make money when you buy and whether they're rushing you, and also whether they show their losses. Follower count or how confident they sound says nothing about whether they know how to invest.

u32l5-8.prompt: To give you personalised advice, you need ____ from the CNMV.
options: a course
advertising
a video
authorisation
u32l5-8.explanation: Recommending what to buy based on your situation is a regulated investment service.

u32l5-10.prompt: A YouTuber with 2 million subscribers says you must buy a share NOW, and Lumi believes him. What do you say?
options: Buy, but only with half your savings
If he says it so confidently, buy
Check whether he's paid to say it
u32l5-10.explanation: Before listening to someone, ask yourself what they gain from you buying.
feedback: Half your savings because of a video is still far too much.
Confidence sells, but it isn't right any more often. And maybe he already owns it and wants you to push the price up.
Nice! Conflicts of interest and pressure are two signs to watch for.
lines: A YouTuber says you have to buy this share NOW 📈
He's got 2 million subscribers, so he definitely knows.

u32l6-1.prompt: Put in order what to do if you've been scammed.
options: Tell your bank
Report it to the police or the Guardia Civil
Keep all the evidence
Stop sending money
Notify the CNMV
u32l6-1.explanation: First stop the bleeding, then document it and report it.

u32l6-6.prompt: What evidence is worth keeping? Select all that apply.
options: Transfer receipts
Nothing: without a signed contract it's no use
Other users' opinions on forums
Screenshots of chats and messages
u32l6-6.explanation: Keep the transfer receipts and screenshots of chats and messages, as well as the website address. Forum opinions don't prove your case, and without evidence, reporting it and making any claim are much harder.

u32l6-8.prompt: Legitimate help or a second scam?
options: INCIBE's 017 gives you free guidance
Complaining to your bank's customer service department
The police or Guardia Civil take your report
A «lawyer» who contacts you first and asks you to pay upfront
A website that claims to recover stolen crypto in exchange for a fee
u32l6-8.explanation: Anyone who contacts you unprompted and charges you upfront to recover your money is suspicious.

u32l6-9.prompt: You have a problem with an authorised broker. Where do you complain first?
options: On its social media
Straight to court, with a lawyer at your side
To the broker's own customer service department
u32l6-9.explanation: It's the mandatory first step; if they don't respond or don't side with you, you can go to the CNMV.

u32l6-10.explanation: 112 is for emergencies and 091 is the Policía Nacional; 016 supports victims of gender-based violence.
